responseSet.title: Hidden Secrets: Between an Attentive Ear and a Containing Mind
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Hidden Secrets: Between an Attentive Ear and a Containing Mind

Hagit Aharoni MA

Hagit Aharoni

Email: gigi_@netvision.net.il

Hagit Aharoni   Clinical psychologist and training psychoanalyst in private practice in Tel Aviv, Israel, where she mainly treats adults in psychoanalytic psychotherapy and serves as a supervising analyst. She is a senior member of the Israel Psychoanalytic Society and the International Psychoanalytical Association, and teaches and supervises at the Israel Psychoanalytic Institute and the Israel Winnicott Center. Her clinical and theoretical interests include trauma, family secrets, birth and growth processes, and Winnicottian perspectives at the interface of literature and psychoanalysis. She has been involved in translating and editing psychoanalytic books into Hebrew and frequently lectures and publishes on contemporary psychoanalytic thought.

The author examines secrets as elements of psychic life and secretiveness as a factor in developmental experience and the formation of selfhood, while also considering conditions under which a secret becomes a painful and tormenting burden. Although a secret is typically defined as content a person does not wish to reveal, the author argues that, in its inner, dynamic nature, a pathogenic secret is better understood as conscious material that could not be heard or contained by a significant other. The secret is conceptualized as a thread leading to primitive, unconscious experiences linked to failures of containment and as a psychic “capsule” whose structure both preserves and confines unprocessed experience. The secrecy mechanism is related to more primitive forms of encapsulation. Using a contemporary literary text and a detailed psychoanalytic treatment, the author illustrates how such secrets may organize individual and familial life and how, within the transference–countertransference relationship, an attentive and containing analytic stance can facilitate the transformation of a tormenting secret into shared meaning and potential psychic change.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Not Before They are Hanged: Working with Revenge

David Dumais LCSW CGP

David Dumais

Email: groupworksfe@gmail.com

David Dumais   Psychotherapist with over thirty years of experience in hospitals, clinics, schools and private practice. He is currently on the faculty of the Center for Group Studies, and provides training and group leadership for the American Groups Psychotherapy Association (AGPA). David has developed an international focus, working primarily with therapists from Russia and China. David maintains offices in both Brooklyn and Manhattan, working with individuals, couples, families and groups.

The author explores revenge as a complex response to injury that blends affect, fantasy, and action, drawing on psychoanalytic theory alongside literary treatments of vengefulness. Revenge is framed on a spectrum from more bounded, reality-tethered efforts at redress to chronic vindictiveness shaped by narcissistic injury, envy, and defensive refusal of loss. Brief clinical vignettes from individual, couple, and group work illustrate how revenge may preserve attachment to the offending object, destabilize self–other boundaries, and intensify countertransference pressures, while raising technical questions about interpretation, survival of attack, and the timely use of limits. The paper was first presented in December 2024 to the Center for Modern Analysis in St. Petersburg, Russia.

“A Salad Bar Approach to Life”: A Study of Defiance and its Uses

Helen Michael PsyaD

Helen Michael

Email: helenmichael@aol.com

Helen Michael   Faculty of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (BGSP). She is Director of the Therapy Center at BGSP, where she is a training analyst, and clinical and research supervisor. Her paper about the unconscious fantasies of fiction writers, “How Writers Write,” was published in 2015 in Psychoanalytic Psychology. Her private practice is in Brookline, Massachusetts.

This paper examines the defiant behavior of a woman who rebelled against all aspects of the treatment contract. It is understood that defiance allowed for safe discharge of sadism and was related defensively to the need for control and to the avoidance of feelings of vulnerability and inferiority. The patient's behavior in sessions is seen as an enactment of her intrapsychic struggle to remain intact. Defiance provided structure, allowing her to maintain herself as separate while staying connected through fighting. Only toxicity was syntonic and could be taken in since cooperation suggested being taken over and ceasing to exist. Defiance was self-destructive yet perceived by the patient to be life-affirming. Clinical challenges for the analyst included tolerating powerful induced feelings of incompetence and accepting the patient's need to maintain defensive opposition.

Michaela Chamberlain

Michaela Chamberlain

Michaela Chamberlain   Trained at the Bowlby Centre and studied in the Psychoanalysis Unit at University College Lodon (UCL). Shortly after qualifying at the Bowlby Centre in 2016, she started teaching Freud and Attachment Theory and became Chair of the Bowlby Centre. She worked as an honorary psychotherapist in two National Health Service (NHS) Trusts for several years. She has presented clinical papers at public forums, lectures internationally and has been published in the British Journal of Psychotherapy, Attachment: New Directions in Psychotherapy and Relational Psychoanalysis, New Associations and The New Psychotherapist Magazine. Her book, Misogyny in Psychoanalysis, was released in June 2022, her latest book, On Resisting Women will be released in February 2026. She is in private practice in London as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and is a supervisor and training therapist.

This paper examines misogyny as an internalized structure affecting individua subjectivity, analytic process, and psychoanalytic training. The author conceptualizes the “misogynistic introject” as a set of identifications and affects that may organize shame, rage, dependency, and desire, and that can shape transference–countertransference configurations in clinical work. The discussion considers how misogyny may be reproduced institutionally when treated as a secondary social issue rather than a constitutive psychic problem. Implications are drawn for training practices, theoretical sources, and clinical attention to gendered authority, harm, and recognition.

Michaela Chamberlain and Michael Sendrow MA LP

Michael Sendrow

Michael Sendrow   Graduate of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS), where he serves as Extension Division Director and is a member of the teaching faculty and Conference Committee. His essays have appeared in various online publications, and his paper, “Just below the surface: The creative expression of psychosomatic symptoms,” was published in Modern Psychoanalysis. Creativity—namely, writing and music—has played an important role in both his self-analysis and psychoanalytic research. He is in private practice in New York City.

Following the presentation of her paper, “The Misogynistic Introject,” the author engages with participants in a question-and-answer discussion that examines the place of misogyny in contemporary psychoanalytic theory, clinical practice, and training. The dialogue considers how misogynistic fantasies, affects, and institutional norms may be reproduced or challenged within analytic settings and within the wider social field. Particular attention is given to how misogyny may be implicated in the structuring of individual subjectivity and in the transmission of psychoanalytic ideas. The participants explore potential directions for revising psychoanalytic education and practice, including the use of alternative source materials, modifications in training methods, and approaches to fostering greater awareness of gendered dynamics in the analytic relationship. The discussion aims to open a space for ongoing inquiry into misogyny as a central, rather than peripheral, concern for psychoanalysis.

The Suicidal Caretaker: Living-Deadness and Mutual Survival

Michael Sendrow MA LP

Michael Sendrow

Email: msendrow@cmps.edu

Michael Sendrow   Graduate of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS), where he serves as Extension Division Director and is a member of the teaching faculty and Conference Committee. His essays have appeared in various online publications, and his paper, “Just below the surface: The creative expression of psychosomatic symptoms,” was published in Modern Psychoanalysis. Creativity—namely, writing and music—has played an important role in both his self-analysis and psychoanalytic research. He is in private practice in New York City.

This paper revisits Green's “dead mother” through the treatment of a patient bound to a dependent, ambivalent parent. The author introduces livingdeadness to describe a stalled psychic state organized by an internal “suicidal caretaker,” an object configuration marked by chronic indecision in which neither separation nor mourning can be sustained. Clinical material shows how this inertia enters the transference–countertransference and progressively immobilizes the analyst. A moment of unexpected suicidal ideation in the analyst is examined as a countertransference communication that clarifies the patient's internal dilemma and shifts the analytic field. Recognizing the suicidal caretaker is presented as a way of loosening the deadlock and restoring movement toward agency and differentiation.

From Breakdown to Breakthrough: Psychoanalytic Treatment of Psychosis, by Danielle Knafo and Michael Selzer. Routledge, 2023. 282 pp.

Nathaniel Cunningham

Nathaniel Cunningham

Nathaniel Cunningham  

In today's clinical landscape, the psychodynamic treatment of psychosis is rare and often dismissed as inappropriate. This shift reflects not only institutional trends but also a deeper discomfort among therapists with the unpredictability and intensity of psychosis. As a consequence, when psychosis “abruptly enters the treatment room—and it often does” (Knafo and Selzer, p. xvi)—many clinicians are unprepared to engage meaningfully with the symptoms and instead either focus on pharmaceutical management or refer the patient elsewhere.

Resisting this prevailing trend in the field, Danielle Knafo and Michael Selzer wrote From Breakdown to Breakthrough to “share [their] experiences with those who wish to learn how to conduct psychodynamic psychotherapy with individuals diagnosed with psychosis or who are undergoing a psychotic episode” (p. xvii). The authors are seasoned clinicians with a century of experience between them, and they describe their book as a “training guide” (p. xvii) for mental health professionals who want to have a better understanding of how to work with states of extreme emotional distress.

Avner Bergstein   Training and supervising psychoanalyst and a faculty member of the Israel Psychoanalytic Society. He maintains a private practice working with adults, adolescents, and children and has worked for several years in a kindergarten for children with autism. He has authored numerous papers exploring the clinical implications of Bion's and Meltzer's writings and is the author of Bion and Meltzer's Expeditions into unmapped mental life: Beyond the spectrum in psychoanalysis (Routledge, 2019). Examining the psychoanalytic process as a means of expanding the mind's capacity for truthfully apprehending reality in its most complex and elusive forms, the author discusses a mode of analytic thinking that moves beyond the linear transformation of unconscious material into conscious awareness. The analytic encounter is described as a space in which both analyst and patient navigate the dynamic tension between the finite and the infinite, the known and the unknowable. In conversation with developments in Quantum Theory, Bion's ideas are used to conceptualize reality as inherently indeterminate and resistant to complete apprehension. The author frames the analytic process not only as a method for uncovering unconscious thoughts buried in the past, but also as a means of cultivating a generative state of mind, oriented toward the future and the unknown, capable of tolerating ambiguity and fostering the emergence of new thought.

Danielle Knafo PHD

Danielle Knafo

danielleknafo@gmail.com

Danielle Knafo   Clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst with expertise in the treatment of psychosis. At Long Island University's clinical psychology doctoral program, she chaired a concentration on serious mental illness. She is on the faculty and a supervisor at NYU's Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis. She has written and lectured extensively on psychoanalysis, trauma, and psychosis. Her most recent book is From breakdown to breakthrough: Psychoanalytic treatment of psychosis (Routledge, 2024).

Through close clinical observation, this paper considers how psychotic symptoms may serve as efforts to manage unbearable affect and relational dislocation. The author offers detailed vignettes to illustrate a treatment stance rooted in responsiveness to the patient's experience, where safety and attunement take precedence over interpretive urgency. Particular attention is given to the ways hallucinations and delusions can convey psychic meaning, often reflecting underlying needs for contact, protection, and continuity. Rather than imposing a unified theory, the paper outlines a flexible, patient-centered approach that privileges collaboration, respects the logic within the symptom, and views the therapeutic relationship as a potential site of anchoring and repair.

Conceptualizing psychosis not as a clinical disorder, the author frames it instead as a developmental position marked by disrupted links between inner experience and the social world. Drawing on psychoanalytic theory, from Lacan's notion of the psychotic position to Bion's emphasis on learning from experience, the author argues that psychotic symptoms often reflect unarticulated trauma and intergenerational transmission of meaning. Through clinical vignettes, the paper illustrates how psychoanalysis can offer a reparative space for symbolic integration by engaging the transference/countertransference field. The work emphasizes the importance of developmental attunement, epistemic trust, and cultural context in supporting those marginalized by medicalized understandings of madness.

Through a series of vignettes and fragments, the author explores everyday psychoses inherent in human life. Working under a conceptual framework of “outside/inside,” the nature of psychosis is observed in clinical experiences, primate behavior, the liminal space between dream, memory and consciousness and evolutionary development. Expanding on Bion's “containment,” Winnicott's “holding” and her own theories on prehistoric human development, she finds metaphor to be the sustaining human adaptation that colors it all. The paper presents a mosaic culled from the author's nonlinear method, revealing impressions, thoughts and the meaning of memories.

Reading, Righting and Unique States of Being

Tim Foljahn MA LP

Tim Foljahn

tfoljahn@yahoo.com

Tim Foljahn   Practicing psychoanalyst in New York City. A graduate of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS) as well as the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, Foljahn is also a musician and visual artist. He was previously an associate editor for Modern Psychoanalysis and is now the newest editor in chief of this publication.

What happens when writing is not merely a task but a state of mind? The author, and editor of this journal, explores writing and reading as immersive and relational experiences that echo the psychoanalytic process. These acts are not simply ways to transmit information, but they are expressions of inner life that shape and reshape the self. The author argues that writing becomes a form of dreaming, a practice of reverie and containment that tries to preserve the many layers of thought. Reading is imagined as a creative encounter in which the reader and text are more actively engaged than is traditionally admitted to or allowed. Drawing from Bion, Bollas, Winnicott, and Ogden, the author proposes that analytic writing ideally produces a space where thinking is altered through the act of expression. As the newest editor of Modern Psychoanalysis, this editor in chief offers the journal as a place that welcomes these transformations, allowing writers and readers to meet through language in a shared pursuit of meaning and psychic discovery.

Among the many accounts of Tiresias in Greek mythology, I first heard the version where Hera and Zeus are arguing about who experiences greater sexual pleasure, with Hera insisting that men do. Tiresias, having been turned into a woman for seven years as a punishment for killing a pair of copulating snakes, seems well-suited to settle the dispute. Apollodorus notes that Tiresias answered: “Of ten parts a man enjoys one only; / But a woman enjoys the full ten parts in her heart.”1 Hera, enraged at being wrong, strikes Tiresias blind. Zeus takes pity on him, but because one God cannot undo the actions of another, Zeus gives him the gift of prophecy as a compensation. This reconciling of ostensible oppositions (punishment—recompense) seems apt for Tiresias as a figure that embodies male and female, mortality and immortality, blindness and insight. Put differently, Tiresias exposes a zone in which so-called opposing terms become indiscernible from one another.

Tiresias is a familiar character in Greek tragedies. Perhaps most famously, he appears as a seer in Sophocles' Oedipus Rex, where he's called upon to answer Oedipus' question about why a plague has beset Thebes. Bits of Psyche: Selected Seminars of Michael Eigen, by Michael Eigen. Routledge. 2024. 320 pp.

Paul Moore

Paul Moore

Paul Moore  

“Whoops—I hear someone saying nothing is always the same. But no, nothing varies too.”

— Eigen, The Psychotic Core, p. 49

Bits of Psyche (2024) is a collection of seven continuous seminars by Michael Eigen. For fifty years, he has been offering these seminars, which have studied Winnicott, Lacan, Bion, and his own material. Having attended some of the seminars, I find that this collection captures what it is like to attend the seminars and provides insight into Eigen's creative force. Eigen has published over 27 books and numerous articles. He relies on the great thinkers of psychoanalysis and history yet retains his own authentic spirit. At 88, Eigen often remarks about how he is still working on himself, still trying to get to know himself, still trying to grow. Eigen is not afraid of free-association and he uses it to gain access to places that might be harder to reach through formalization. He integrates his own experiences with the texts that he is teaching and provides highly original outside sources from literature, religion, philosophy and poetry. He also makes connections between the readings he assigns and the current political atmosphere, linking intrapsychic processes with political processes. Recently, Eigen has dedicated most of his seminars to studying Bion's A Memoir of the Future (1991). Each week the group is assigned a section of the text and then it is discussed during the seminar. In essence, Bits of Psyche is about Eigen teaching the group about this often-ignored text. While A Memoir of the Future is the main text, Eigen pulls from the entire corpus of Bion's work.

From the chosen seminars, I want to focus on his work on self-states, numbing processes, and the relation between self, other and war. In the seminars, Eigen will sometimes tell the group to say hello to themselves. The assumption is that one would not need to do that, one is already there.

Remembering Faye Newsome

Faye Newsome passed away on Saturday, May 24th, at the age of 83. Her loss is felt deeply by those who knew her, as a colleague, a friend, and a vital force in the life of The Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS).

Faye was part of the Center from the beginning, first as a student, then as a training analyst, supervisor, faculty member, Editor-in-Chief of Modern Psychoanalysis, and Chair of the Board of Trustees. Her intelligence was unmistakable, precise, unsentimental, and animated by a genuine curiosity about the human condition. She asked good questions and expected good answers, and her dedication to the Center helped shape it into what it is today.

As editor, Faye took the helm of the journal with a clear vision and a deep sense of responsibility after the passing of the torch from June Bernstein. Faye led with decisiveness and care, keeping the journal intellectually lively and clinically grounded. Her own writing, including pieces like “Envy and the Negative Therapeutic Reaction”, reflected a mind that was both sharp and steady. She contributed to the field, but never in a way that called attention to itself.
